cases.abstract: DROID is a manipulation-data resource designed to expand scene coverage while keeping distributed collection reproducible. It pairs a dataset with a portable robot platform shared by 13 institutions. Collectors calibrate cameras for each scene, specify feasible tasks, and execute randomly assigned tasks through VR teleoperation; periodic changes to viewpoints, lighting, clutter, and robot placement extend coverage. The dataset contains 76,000 successful episodes across 564 scenes in 52 buildings, accompanied by collection and policy-training resources. Utility is evaluated with existing language-conditioned diffusion policies trained separately for six tasks at four locations on the shared hardware. Mixing successful DROID trajectories equally with in-domain demonstrations yields mean success rates 22 percentage points above the next-best method in-distribution and 17 points above it under task-specific distribution shifts. Comparators use the same backbone with in-domain data alone or a 50/50 mixture of in-domain and curated Open X-Embodiment data. At a fixed subset size, broader scene coverage also improves performance on the challenging shifted tasks studied, supporting dataset utility alongside continued use of in-domain demonstrations.
cases.methods: DROID combines a common collection setup with deliberate scene variation. A portable Franka Panda robot, two adjustable external stereo cameras, a wrist stereo camera, and VR teleoperation provide the shared setup across institutions. For each scene, collectors calibrate cameras and list feasible tasks; random episode-level assignment and periodic prompts to change viewpoints, lighting, clutter, or base placement encourage coverage beyond easy tasks. Evaluation trains a separate language-conditioned diffusion policy for each of six tasks on this hardware. A 50/50 mixture of successful DROID trajectories and in-domain demonstrations is compared with in-domain-only training and equally mixed co-training with curated Open X-Embodiment data, using the same backbone. Ten rollouts per method and task setting measure success under perturbed initial robot and object positions and task-specific shifts involving distractors, new manipulated objects, or camera placement.
cases.results: Co-training with equal parts successful DROID trajectories and in-domain demonstrations improves mean success across six manipulation tasks relative to in-domain-only training and equally mixed co-training with curated Open X-Embodiment data. With a shared policy backbone and ten rollouts per method and task setting, its mean success exceeds the next-best method by 22 percentage points in-distribution and 17 percentage points on task-specific out-of-distribution variants. A separate comparison asks whether scene coverage matters when demonstration count is fixed. Both subsets contain 7,362 successful demonstrations and are mixed equally with in-domain data; a uniformly sampled, more scene-diverse subset outperforms one drawn from the 20 most represented scenes on the challenging shifted tasks studied. This supports a role for scene coverage beyond subset size, without isolating all other differences between the subsets. The main comparison covers four locations on DROID hardware.

notes.abstract: Selected D01-D02 for reproducible collection with scene variation and D03-D08 for scale and utility. Read-back retains the dataset and platform contribution, existing-policy evaluation, and task-scoped co-training gains; the diversity result does not establish an isolated cause.
notes.methods: Selected D01-D02 and D05-D07 to connect collection consistency, coverage decisions, and policy evaluation. Read-back distinguishes scene variation from shared hardware and identifies matched backbones, mixture ratios, and rollout conditions; the ten-rollout count applies to the main comparison.
notes.results: Selected D06-D08 for the decisive co-training comparison and size-matched diversity check; D05 bounds hardware and location scope. Read-back preserves percentage-point gains over the next-best method and treats diversity as supporting, not uniquely causal, evidence. No significance claim is inferred.

cases.abstract: SIMPLER evaluates policies trained on real robot data in simulation, aiming to recover relative performance and informative behavioral differences rather than exact physical success rates. The framework aligns simulated action effects by replaying existing demonstrations and tuning controller stiffness and damping against end-effector trajectory mismatch. Its default Visual Matching approach reduces visual discrepancies by combining simulated robots and interactive objects with an inpainted real-scene background and adjusting their appearance. Mean Maximum Rank Violation measures misordering by averaging each policy's largest misranking margin measured in real-world success rates. For six policy checkpoints across three Google Robot task groups, Visual Matching gives lower mean rank violation (0.056) than averaging randomized visual variants (0.143) or validation action MSE (0.375). A behavioral check also finds greater arm-texture sensitivity for Octo-Base than RT-1-X in simulation, a relative pattern supported by new physical arm-wrapping experiments. These results support simulation as a policy-comparison signal within the tested rigid-body setups, rather than as a substitute for all real-robot evaluation.
cases.methods: SIMPLER aligns simulated action effects with real demonstrations before comparing policies trained on real data across simulation and hardware. Actions from recorded real demonstrations are replayed in simulation, and simulated annealing adjusts stiffness and damping to reduce discrepancies in end-effector translation and rotation, without collecting new demonstrations for this step. Visual Matching addresses visual mismatch by compositing segmented simulated robots and interactive objects onto an inpainted real-scene background and adjusting or projecting textures. Variant Aggregation provides an alternative that averages outcomes across randomized visual environments. Policies are evaluated in paired simulated and physical Google Robot and WidowX task setups, principally for rigid-body manipulation. Agreement is assessed using Mean Maximum Rank Violation: each policy contributes its worst misranking margin in real-world success rate, and these margins are averaged. Pearson correlation is reported alongside this margin-sensitive measure rather than used as the sole test of ranking agreement.
cases.results: Visual Matching yields the closest agreement with real-world policy rankings among the three evaluation approaches compared for six checkpoints across three Google Robot task groups. Its average Mean Maximum Rank Violation is 0.056, versus 0.143 for Variant Aggregation and 0.375 for validation action MSE; corresponding mean Pearson correlations are 0.924, 0.778, and 0.308. The lower rank violation indicates smaller worst misranking margins on average, and the correlation comparison also favors Visual Matching. A separate robustness check examines whether simulation captures differences in sensitivity, not just aggregate ordering. Simulation suggests Octo-Base is more sensitive to arm texture than RT-1-X, and new real-world arm-wrapping experiments support that relative difference. These comparisons support policy ranking and behavioral diagnosis in the tested rigid-body setups, with agreement judged by relative ordering and sensitivity rather than exact success rates for every policy.

notes.abstract: Selected S01-S05 for relative evaluation, action and visual alignment, and the ranking metric; S07 and S09 test ordering and behavioral sensitivity. Read-back retains the framework and metric contributions without presenting ranking measures as success rates or implying universal simulation fidelity.
notes.methods: Selected S02-S06 to connect action alignment, visual alignment, and paired evaluation. Read-back recovers controller tuning from existing demonstrations, object and robot appearance matching, and per-policy worst-margin averaging. The no-new-demonstration condition applies only to system identification.
notes.results: Selected S07 for the Google Robot comparison and S09 for the physically checked sensitivity pattern. Read-back interprets lower MMRV as smaller average worst misranking margins, not higher robot success, and limits the arm-texture finding to the named policies and tested conditions.
